title: Winslow Homer, Pumpkin Patch (1878)
summary: Five distinct failure modes behind one word, with the papers that separate them: why self-review makes two of them worse, and why only the last one converts a model error into a breach.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**"Hallucination" is doing too much work as a word. It covers five distinct failure modes, and only two of them are the reason agents cause incidents.** A wrong sentence in a chat window and a wrong database write share a root cause and nothing else.


Two of the five have published mechanisms now. Kalai and colleagues argue models guess because benchmarks reward guessing, calling the state of evaluation an "epidemic of penalizing uncertain responses." A separate 2024 paper argues from computability theory that some residual rate survives any amount of training data and coins the term "structural hallucination" for it.


The one that produces incidents is different in kind. Tool and permission hallucinations act instead of stating. And the measurement that should worry anyone hoping to fix this with better models runs the other way: strengthening reasoning through RL raised tool hallucination in step with task performance, and every mitigation tested traded utility for reliability.


We're not claiming model quality is irrelevant. It shrinks three of the five. It does not shrink the fifth, because the gap there isn't knowledge, it's that nothing checked the agent's belief about its own authority against a record outside the model.


So put the authority check outside the model. NIST's zero-trust tenets already say it in one line: authorization is "dynamic and strictly enforced before access is allowed."
